title: Comparatives 2: Than and Degree
summary: Compare people, things and amounts using than. Make differences clearer with a bit and much, and use natural pronouns and clauses after than.
learningObjectives: Connect a comparative adjective or adverb to the second person or thing with than.
Use natural object pronouns after than or make a full comparison clause.
Use more than and less than for amounts, distances and times.
Use a bit and much to describe small and large comparative differences.

explanation.heading: The second part of a comparison: than
explanation.body: Use than to introduce the person or thing used as the comparison. The usual pattern is comparative + than + person/thing: taller than, more expensive than, or faster than. Do not confuse than (comparison) with then (time).
explanation.example: My train is faster than your bus.

explanation.heading: Pronouns and clauses after than
explanation.body: In everyday English, object pronouns are common after than: than me, than him, than her and than them. You can also use a subject with the appropriate verb: than I do, than she can or than he is. Keep the auxiliary verb appropriate to the meaning.
explanation.example: Nora gets up earlier than I do.

explanation.heading: Comparing amounts: more than and less than
explanation.body: More than means above an amount, and less than means below an amount. Use these phrases before numbers, times, prices or distances. You can also use more or less with a comparison when the quantity is understood.
explanation.example: The repair took less than two hours.

explanation.heading: Small and large differences
explanation.body: Place a bit or much before the comparative to show the size of the difference. A bit means a small difference; much means a large one. With longer adjectives, say a bit more useful or much more comfortable. Do not say more taller.
explanation.example: The upstairs room is a bit cooler than the kitchen.

comparisons.title: Two natural ways to compare people

left.label: Object pronoun
left.note: An object pronoun is common in ordinary conversation.

right.label: Full comparison clause
right.example: Ella reads faster than I do.
right.note: Use a subject and a suitable verb.

left.label: Small difference
left.example: This mug is a bit larger than that one.
left.note: A bit indicates a small difference.

right.label: Large difference
right.example: This bottle is much larger than that one.

examples.sentence: My blue trainers are newer than my black ones.
examples.note: Than introduces the second pair of trainers.

examples.sentence: Our dog runs faster than I do.
examples.note: The comparison clause uses the auxiliary do.

examples.sentence: The museum is less than a kilometre away.
examples.note: Less than means below this distance.

examples.sentence: It costs more than twenty pounds to replace the screen.
examples.note: More than introduces an amount above twenty pounds.

examples.sentence: The upstairs bedroom is much quieter than the one below.
examples.note: Much strengthens the comparative and shows a large difference.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Your coat is longer then mine.
commonMistakes.correct: Your coat is longer than mine.
commonMistakes.why: Than introduces comparisons; then usually refers to time or sequence.

commonMistakes.incorrect: This bike is much more faster than mine.
commonMistakes.correct: This bike is much faster than mine.
commonMistakes.why: Do not add more to an adjective already ending in comparative -er.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Her lunch cost less of ten pounds.
commonMistakes.correct: Her lunch cost less than ten pounds.
commonMistakes.why: Use than, not of, after less when comparing an amount.

commonMistakes.incorrect: He swims faster than I am.
commonMistakes.correct: He swims faster than I do.
commonMistakes.why: Use do to refer back to the action swim in a complete comparison clause.

studyTips: When writing a comparative sentence, underline the comparative and circle than to check that the two parts connect.
Remember: than compares; then talks about time or what happens next.
Add a bit for a small difference and much for a large difference, before the comparative form.

exercises.prompt: Mina is 1.60 metres tall and Eva is 1.70 metres tall. Eva is ___ Mina.
exercises.feedback: Eva is taller, and than introduces Mina as the person compared.

exercises.prompt: The green coat costs £50 and the blue one costs £70. The blue coat costs more ___ the green coat.
exercises.feedback: Use than, not then, to introduce the second price.

exercises.prompt: It was 10 degrees yesterday and it is 30 degrees today. Today is ___.
exercises.feedback: Much hotter than expresses a large temperature difference and uses than correctly.

exercises.prompt: The walk takes 25 minutes. Which sentence describes its duration correctly?
choices: The walk takes less than 30 minutes.
The walk takes more than 30 minutes.
exercises.feedback: Twenty-five minutes is less than thirty minutes.

exercises.prompt: The town library is bigger ___ the village library. (comparison word)
exercises.feedback: Than introduces the second library in a comparative sentence.

exercises.prompt: The early train leaves at seven and the late train at eight. The early train leaves an hour ___ than the late train. (early: comparative)
exercises.feedback: Earlier is the comparative of early; than connects the two trains.

exercises.prompt: My sister swims faster than ___. (use the everyday object pronoun for the speaker)
exercises.feedback: Than me is a natural everyday comparison; than I do is also correct when a full clause is used.

exercises.prompt: The blue notebook costs £2.10 and the green one costs £2.00. The blue one is ___ more expensive than the green one. (use a bit or much for a small difference)
exercises.feedback: A bit more expensive describes the small price difference of ten pence.

exercises.prompt: Correct the comparison word only: Jules is taller that his brother.
acceptedAnswers: Jules is taller than his brother.
exercises.feedback: Than, not that, follows a comparative adjective.

exercises.prompt: Correct the comparative phrase only: This novel is a bit more longer than that one.
acceptedAnswers: This novel is a bit longer than that one.
exercises.feedback: Longer already has comparative -er, so remove more; a bit remains.

exercises.prompt: Correct the comparison word only: My new flat costs less then eight hundred pounds a month.
acceptedAnswers: My new flat costs less than eight hundred pounds a month.
exercises.feedback: Less than introduces a price below the stated amount.

exercises.prompt: Correct the auxiliary verb only: Lena runs faster than I am.
acceptedAnswers: Lena runs faster than I do.
exercises.feedback: The auxiliary do refers to the action run: faster than I do.

speakingExercises.prompt: The red bag is heavier. The green bag is lighter. Say one full sentence beginning with "The red bag" and comparing it with "the green bag" using than.
acceptedAnswers: The red bag is heavier than the green bag.
speakingExercises.feedback: A comparative followed by than introduces the other bag.

speakingExercises.prompt: Leo is 21 and Mila is 20. Say a full sentence beginning with "Leo" and using the exact phrase "a bit older than Mila".
acceptedAnswers: Leo is a bit older than Mila.
speakingExercises.feedback: A bit older than describes the small age difference.

speakingExercises.prompt: A train ticket costs £8 and a bus ticket costs £5. Say a complete sentence beginning "The train" and comparing the tickets using "more expensive than the bus".
acceptedAnswers: The train is more expensive than the bus.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use more expensive than to compare the prices.

speakingExercises.prompt: The small bowl has four pears, and the large bowl has seven. Say one full sentence beginning "The large bowl has" and ending "the small bowl". Use "more pears than".
acceptedAnswers: The large bowl has more pears than the small bowl.
speakingExercises.feedback: More pears than compares the number of pears in two bowls.

speakingExercises.prompt: Nina speaks quietly, but Sam speaks loudly. Compare how they speak. Begin "Sam speaks" and end "Nina does". Use "louder than".
acceptedAnswers: Sam speaks louder than Nina does.
speakingExercises.feedback: Than introduces Nina, and does stands for the verb speaks in the comparison clause.

speakingExercises.prompt: You can swim twenty lengths, and Mia can swim thirty. Tell a friend in one sentence beginning "Mia can swim" and ending "me". Use "more lengths than".
acceptedAnswers: Mia can swim more lengths than me.
speakingExercises.feedback: More lengths than me is a natural everyday comparison using an object pronoun.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only one word in this sentence and say the full result: "The bakery is cheaper then the café."
acceptedAnswers: The bakery is cheaper than the café.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use than for comparisons. Then usually describes a time or a sequence.

speakingExercises.prompt: Two buses follow the same route. The express bus takes twenty minutes, and the local bus takes eighty minutes. Tell a visitor how they compare in one sentence beginning "The express bus is". Use "much faster than the local bus".
acceptedAnswers: The express bus is much faster than the local bus.
speakingExercises.feedback: Much faster than describes a large difference in speed on the same route.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our hotel room is a bit brighter than yours.
listeningExercises.prompt: How large is the difference in brightness?
listeningExercises.feedback: A bit brighter expresses a small difference.

listeningExercises.audioText: The journey takes less than forty minutes.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is true about the journey time?
listeningExercises.feedback: Less than forty minutes means under forty minutes.

listeningExercises.audioText: The old bridge is much narrower than the new bridge.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word comparative phrase you hear that emphasises the difference.
listeningExercises.feedback: Much emphasises a large difference, and narrower is the comparative adjective.

listeningExercises.audioText: The smaller backpack costs much less than the larger one, although both look nice.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which backpack would be the cheaper choice?
listeningExercises.feedback: The smaller backpack costs much less, so it is the cheaper choice.

listeningExercises.audioText: The library opens at eight in the morning, but the café opens half an hour later than the library.
listeningExercises.prompt: At what time does the second place open?
listeningExercises.feedback: Half an hour later than eight in the morning is eight thirty.

listeningExercises.audioText: Ben studies a little longer than I do, but Lucy studies much longer than both of us.
listeningExercises.prompt: Who spends the most time studying?
listeningExercises.feedback: Lucy studies much longer than both the speaker and Ben, so she spends the most time studying.

listeningExercises.audioText: The bus will be here in less than ten minutes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression showing the wait is below the stated time.
listeningExercises.feedback: You heard less than, which means below the stated amount of time.

listeningExercises.audioText: My new walking shoes are a bit lighter than the old pair.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression that describes the size of the weight difference.
listeningExercises.feedback: You heard a bit, which describes a small difference before a comparative.
